title: Phishing Attacks
short: Learn how to spot fake emails, links and urgent messages.
description: Phishing is when someone pretends to be a trusted person or company to trick you into sharing information or opening a dangerous link.
example: You receive a message saying your university email will be blocked in one hour unless you enter your password on a new website.
warningSigns: A message creates panic or pressure to act immediately.
The sender address or website spelling looks unusual.
A link asks for a password or personal information unexpectedly.
tips: Open the official website yourself rather than using the message link.
Check the sender and website address carefully.
Report suspicious messages to your university IT staff.
remember: Pause and check before you click.

title: Password Safety
short: Create stronger passwords and protect your accounts.
description: Strong, unique passwords make it harder for attackers to access your accounts. Multi-factor authentication provides another layer of protection.
example: A student uses the same password for social media and the university portal. One leaked password could put both accounts at risk.
warningSigns: You reuse the same password across several websites.
You share a password with friends or classmates.
Your account has no additional sign-in verification.
tips: Use a different long password or passphrase for each account.
Use a trusted password manager if available.
Enable multi-factor authentication when offered.

title: Malware & Viruses
short: Avoid harmful apps, files and unexpected downloads.
description: Malware is harmful software that can steal information, damage files or disrupt a device. It may arrive through unsafe downloads or suspicious attachments.
example: A free software installer from an unknown website asks you to disable antivirus protection before running it.
warningSigns: Pop-up messages demand you install unknown software.
A download comes from an untrusted website.
Your device suddenly shows unusual behavior after an installation.
tips: Download apps from official or trusted sources.
Keep your operating system and applications updated.
Scan suspicious files and do not disable security tools casually.
remember: Think carefully before installing unknown files.

title: Safe Web Browsing
short: Browse carefully and recognize misleading websites.
description: Safe browsing means checking websites, links and downloads so that you avoid scams and protect your personal data.
example: A shopping page has a nearly correct brand name and asks for a bank card even though the offer looks too good to be true.
warningSigns: The website address looks like a misspelled brand.
A site asks for unrelated private details.
An offer seems unrealistic or pushes an immediate payment.
tips: Type the official website address when possible.
Look at the full website address, not just the page design.
Remember that HTTPS alone does not prove a site is trustworthy.
remember: A professional-looking website can still be a scam.

title: Social Engineering
short: Recognize tricks that use trust, fear or curiosity.
description: Social engineering uses human emotions and trust to persuade people to reveal information or perform unsafe actions.
example: A caller claims to be from campus IT and asks you to read out the sign-in code that was sent to your phone.
warningSigns: Someone demands a one-time verification code.
A caller uses authority or urgency to pressure you.
A stranger asks you to ignore normal verification steps.
tips: Verify unexpected requests using a trusted contact method.
Never share one-time sign-in codes.
Ask university staff when you are unsure about a request.
remember: Verify the person, not just the story.

title: Device Security
short: Protect laptops and phones used for university work.
description: Device security includes keeping software updated, locking screens and protecting files from unwanted access.
example: You leave your unlocked laptop in the library while you go to get lunch.
warningSigns: Your device does not require a screen lock.
You often postpone important security updates.
Sensitive files are stored without a backup.
tips: Use a PIN, password or biometric screen lock.
Install updates from trusted system settings.
Back up important study files regularly.
remember: Lock it before you leave it.

title: Data Privacy
short: Know what personal data you share with apps.
description: Data privacy means understanding and controlling how your personal information is collected, used and shared.
example: A simple calculator app asks for access to your contacts and location even though it does not need them to work.
warningSigns: An app requests permissions unrelated to its purpose.
A form asks for sensitive details without explaining why.
You post a student ID number or other private information publicly.
tips: Review permissions before granting access.
Share only the information that is needed.
Check privacy settings on social media and apps.

title: Public Wi-Fi Safety
short: Stay careful when using shared networks.
description: Public Wi-Fi can be convenient but unfamiliar networks may expose you to fake hotspots or insecure connections.
example: At a café, you find two similarly named networks and cannot tell which one belongs to the café.
warningSigns: A network name imitates a familiar place.
A login page asks for unnecessary private details.
Your device joins unfamiliar networks automatically.
tips: Ask staff for the correct Wi-Fi name when unsure.
Avoid sensitive activity on unknown or suspicious networks.
Turn off automatic joining of unfamiliar networks.
